newsitem.title: UK: POLL-Few expected to attain EMU guidelines.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Few expected to attain EMU guidelines.

text.p: Politics rather than economics still leads Europe's quest for a single currency, with few countries coming close to meeting all of the economic targets set for the launch of the euro, a Reuters poll showed on Wednesday.

Forecasts from 23 economists across Europe showed that all European Union (EU) countries except France had closed in slightly over the past three months on the economic convergence targets for membership of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

But the poll, conducted between August 6 and 8, showed that the slow drift in the right economic direction would be strong enough to carry only two countries, Finland and Luxembourg, far enough to meet the criteria laid out in the Maastricht Treaty.

EMU candidates must aim to meet targets covering budget deficit and public debt in relation to size of gross domestic product (GDP), together with low inflation and interest rates and currency stability.

"EMU will prevail in the end, so long as there is a political will. Mechanically it would have been impossible for some countries to have reduced their budget deficits enough to meet the Maastricht targets," said Steven Englander, international economist at Smith Barney in Paris.
"The (treaty's) good faith clause will have to be invoked," he said.
According to the survey, France was still pulling the wrong way, its budget deficit-to-GDP ratio creeping upwards despite pledges of fiscal austerity from the government.

The median of 19 forecasts showed France's budget deficit-to-GDP ratio, which the Maastricht treaty says should be three percent or less during 1997, was expected to be 3.30 percent, compared with 3.05 percent three months ago.
France would meet its other economic targets, the median findings of the survey showed.

Germany, waging its own battle to bring down its budget deficit, remained at a static 3.20 percent compared with the Reuters May poll, and 20 economists made an average prediction of nearly 62 percent for its public debt-to-GDP ratio, largely unchanged from three months ago and obstinately on the wrong side of the 60 percent Maastricht target.

Analysts said the absolute necessity of having Europe's economic powerhouse as a core member of the EMU club and its glowing economic track record before reunification would carry the day for German membership.

But they said that the relative unpopularity of a single currency in Germany, particularly if a weaker, broader euro took over from a strong mark, might sound Chancellor Helmut Kohl's political death knell.
"Herr Kohl wants to make history once again, not only with reunification but with monetary union," said Niels Kortleve, analyst with Rabobank in the Netherlands.
"The election could pose problems for Kohl but it will not be a problem for EMU. Our view is that all decisions on EMU will have been made by the time of the German election," he said.
Kohl, his government currently sliding badly in the opinion polls, faces re-election next September.

Britain is expected to fulfil all of the Maastricht economic criteria, but was seen falling short on the currency stability rules because it is not a member of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Ireland, the Netherlands, Spain, Portugal and Sweden were all deemed in the survey to fall short of the Maastricht public debt targets, while the analysts predicted that Italy would fall short of both debt and budget deficit criteria. Sweden, like Britain, remains outside the ERM currency grid.
Once again, all contributors to the survey predicted that Greece would fail all of the convergence criteria.
